**Answer: $\mathrm{ex}_L(n,P_5)=\frac{16n}{11}$ when $11\mid n$.** I did not fully verify this, so treat it as a well-motivated estimate rather than a proof.

**Why 11-vertex blocks.** $P_5$ has $3\cdot5-4=11$ vertices, so any linear 3-graph whose connected components each have at most 10 vertices is automatically $P_5$-free. The extremal construction is then a disjoint union of copies of one best block. The condition $11\mid n$ suggests the block has 11 vertices.

**Comparing candidate blocks.**
- A 10-vertex block gives at most $D(10,3,2)=13$ edges, a density of $13/10=1.3$.
- For an 11-vertex block with $c$ edges to beat this, we need $c/11>1.3$, i.e. $c\ge 15$.

**Ruling out 17.** The maximum packing on 11 points has 17 triples. I built one such packing and found an explicit spanning $P_5$ in it:
$\{a,3,6\},\{c,4,6\},\{1,4,5\},\{d,1,7\},\{b,d,2\}$.
Consecutive edges meet in one vertex and non-consecutive edges are disjoint. I checked only this one construction, so this rules out 17 for that packing; I did not prove that every 17-edge packing contains a $P_5$.

**Choosing 16.** The value $c=16$ is the natural candidate: it exceeds the 10-vertex density and is the next value below 17. I did not construct a 16-edge $P_5$-free block or prove the matching upper bound $\mathrm{ex}_L(n,P_5)\le 16n/11$. This is the step most in need of verification.

Under this reasoning, $\mathrm{ex}_L(n,P_5)=\frac{16n}{11}$.

ANSWER: $\frac{16n}{11}$
